1H (Number Theory)

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 86
1H OurBigBook.com
Expand the finite Euler product into convergent geometric series. Every positive integer n≤x has all its prime factors at most x, so
P(x)−1=∏p≤x​∑k≥0​p−k=∑n≥1all prime factors of n≤x​​n1​≥∑n≤x​n1​.
(1)
The harmonic series diverges, hence P(x)→0. If the sum of reciprocal primes were finite, then the inequality −log(1−t)≤2t for 0≤t≤1/2 would give
−logP(x)=∑p≤x​−log(1−1/p)≤2∑p​p1​<∞,
(2)
uniformly in x, contradicting P(x)→0. Thus the sum of prime reciprocals diverges. Unique factorization justifies the expansion; no estimate for the distribution of primes is required. This is the Euler proof that the sum of reciprocals of primes diverges.

a OurBigBook.com
The closed-set form of the Baire category theorem says: if a nonempty complete metric space is a countable union of closed sets, at least one of those sets has nonempty interior. Equivalently, a complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interiors. In the application the space is R with its usual complete metric.

Solution

Words: 113
b OurBigBook.com
Suppose the continuous functions converged pointwise to the rationality indicator. Each FN​ is closed, since
FN​=⋂n≥N​(fn−1​((−∞,1/3])∪fn−1​([2/3,∞))).
(3)
Pointwise convergence implies that every point belongs to some FN​: its eventual values lie near either zero or one. Thus R=⋃N​FN​. By the Baire category theorem, some FN​ contains a nonempty open interval I. Choose a rational r∈I and an irrational s∈I. For sufficiently large n≥N, convergence gives fn​(r)>2/3 and fn​(s)<1/3. The intermediate value theorem then forces fn​ to take the value 1/2 between them, at a point in I⊆FN​. This contradicts the defining condition of FN​. Therefore the rationality indicator is not a pointwise limit of continuous functions, the rationality indicator is not Baire class one result.

3F (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 305 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 305
3F OurBigBook.com
A plane crystallographic group is a discrete subgroup of the Euclidean plane's isometry group with compact quotient; equivalently a compact set has translates covering the plane. We prove the crystallographic restriction theorem without assuming its conclusion. The orientation-preserving subgroup G+ has index at most two and still has a cocompact group action. Its subgroup T of translations is discrete as an additive subgroup of R2.
Suppose T were trivial. Linear parts of orientation-preserving plane isometries commute, so every group commutator in G+ is a translation. Thus G+ would be an abelian group. Every member would then commute with the given nontrivial rotation g and preserve its unique fixed point. A discrete subgroup of the compact rotation group about that point is finite. Then G would be finite, contradicting cocompactness on the unbounded plane. Hence T contains a nonzero vector v.
If g is a half-turn its order is already two. Otherwise its linear part R rotates v to a linearly independent vector Rv, and conjugating translations shows that Rv∈T. Thus T spans the plane and is a euclidean lattice. A discrete additive subgroup meets every bounded closed set in finitely many points: an accumulating sequence would give nonzero differences tending to zero, contradicting isolation of the identity. To see the euclidean lattice assertion directly, choose a shortest nonzero translation v. Translations on its line are integer multiples of v. Reducing all parallel components modulo v shows that nonzero perpendicular components are bounded away from zero, since otherwise infinitely many translation vectors would accumulate in a compact rectangle. Choose a vector w with the smallest positive perpendicular component; reducing by w and then v proves T=Zv+Zw.
Conjugation by g preserves this euclidean lattice. In its euclidean lattice basis, R is therefore an invertible integer matrix with determinant one. Its trace is an integer and is also 2cosθ, where θ is the rotation angle. Since g is nontrivial,
2cosθ∈{−2,−1,0,1}.
(4)
These values give angles of order 2,3,4,6 respectively. Hence
ord(g)∈{2,3,4,6}​.
(5)

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 95
4G OurBigBook.com
Shannon second coding theorem identifies the channel capacity of a discrete memoryless channel as C=maxPX​​I(X;Y): rates below C admit block codes with error probability tending to zero, whereas a rate above C cannot achieve vanishing error. Entropies here are measured in bits. For a binary erasure channel, a non-erased output determines its input exactly, while an erasure, independent of the input, leaves the original uncertainty unchanged. If P(X=1)=q, then
H(X)=h2​(q),H(X∣Y)=ph2​(q),I(X;Y)=(1−p)h2​(q).
(6)
The binary entropy function has maximum one at q=1/2. Therefore
C=1−p bits per channel use​.
(7)
This includes the noiseless case p=0 and the wholly erased case p=1.

Solution

Words: 234
5I OurBigBook.com
The R command fits a Poisson regression with the default log link:
Yi​∼Poisson(λi​),logλi​=β0​+β1​Ti​,
(8)
with independent annual counts conditional on the supplied temperature index. The fitted mean is λ(T)=exp(2.26061+0.48870T). The intercept gives about 9.59 expected named storms at index zero. A one-unit increase in the index multiplies the expected count by e0.48870≃1.63; a 0.1 increase multiplies it by about 1.050.
The reported standard errors estimate the sampling uncertainty of the coefficients. Each displayed z is the estimate divided by its standard error, compared with a standard normal distribution under a zero-coefficient null hypothesis. The slope has z=2.879 and two-sided p=0.00399, evidence of positive association within this model. The intercept test is against mean one at index zero and is not itself a test of a climatic mechanism. Association does not establish causation.
There are 61 annual observations and two fitted coefficients, giving 59 residual degrees of freedom. The residual deviance is
2∑i​[Yi​log(Yi​/λi​)−(Yi​−λi​)]=51.499,
(9)
with 0log0=0. It is not large relative to 59 and gives no obvious overdispersion signal, although temporal dependence and omitted covariates still require substantive assessment.
For 2005 insert the index into the fitted mean:
λ2005​=e2.26061+0.48870(0.743)≃13.79​.
(10)
This is an expected count, approximately fourteen storms, rather than a guarantee of an integer outcome. In R one would use predict(Mod, newdata=data.frame(Temp=0.743), type="response"). A predictive distribution must include Poisson variation and, if desired, coefficient-estimation uncertainty; the latter needs the coefficient covariance matrix, not just the two printed standard errors.

7E OurBigBook.com
The nonzero fixed point of the logistic map is x∗​=(μ−1)/μ, with multiplier F′(x∗​)=2−μ. It is stable for 1<μ<3, and its multiplier crosses −1 at μ=3. To identify the emerging orbit explicitly, factor
F2(x)−x=−x(μx−μ+1)[μ2x2−μ(μ+1)x+μ+1].
(18)
The remaining two roots, interchanged by F, are
x1,2​=2μμ+1±(μ+1)(μ−3)​​​.
(19)
They coincide with x∗​ at three and are distinct for μ>3. Their cycle multiplier is
Λ2​=F′(x1​)F′(x2​)=μ2(1−2x1​)(1−2x2​)=−μ2+2μ+4.
(20)
It lies between −1 and 1 for 3<μ<1+6​. This establishes the first period-doubling bifurcation and the stable bifurcating two-cycle.
At μ2​=1+6​, Λ2​=−1 and dΛ2​/dμ=−26​=0. The second flip is nondegenerate: for H=F2 at either cycle point, the cubic flip coefficient is c=(H′′′/6)+(H′′/2)2=−SH/6 when H′=−1. Here S denotes the Schwarzian derivative. Since SF=−6/(1−2x)2<0 and S(F2)=(SF∘F)(F′)2+SF, this coefficient is positive. Locally, after following the fixed point of H, its second iterate has the form H2(y)−y=2a(μ−μ2​)y−2cy3+⋯, with a=26​>0. Nonzero roots therefore appear with y2∼a(μ−μ2​)/c on the increasing-parameter side. These are a four-cycle of F, proving the second period-doubling bifurcation occurs at μ=1+6​.

For Rez>0, absolute convergence permits the two-dimensional gamma integral
Γ(z/2)2=∫0∞​∫0∞​e−(u+v)uz/2−1vz/2−1dudv.
(21)
Put u=rs, v=r(1−s), with r>0, 0<s<1 and Jacobian determinant r. Separation of the integrals gives the beta--gamma identity
Γ(z/2)2=Γ(z)B(z/2,z/2)​.
(22)
The beta integral is finite in this half-plane. Thus a zero of Γ(z) would imply Γ(z/2)=0, and iteration would imply Γ(z/2m)=0 for every positive integer m. But integration by parts gives wΓ(w)=Γ(1+w), and continuity near one makes Γ(1+w)→1 as w→0. It cannot vanish for sufficiently small w, a contradiction. Therefore the Gamma function has no zeros in the right half-plane.
For any z outside the nonpositive integers, choose an integer n with Re(z+n)>0. The Gamma function recurrence gives
Γ(z)=z(z+1)⋯(z+n−1)Γ(z+n)​=0.
(23)
At the excluded integers gamma has poles, with nonzero residues by the same recurrence. Hence the meromorphic gamma function has no zeros anywhere; at its poles it has no finite value to which a nonzero-value assertion could apply.

Ix​=Iy​=M(4R2​+3h2​),Iz​=2MR2​​.
(24)

R2h​=3​​

In the nonrelativistic dilute regime, E(p)=mc2+p2/(2m)+⋯ and the Fermi-Dirac distribution reduces to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Hence
n≃h34π​e(μ−mc2)/(kT)∫0∞​p2e−p2/(2mkT)dp.
(26)
Differentiating the Gaussian integral with respect to its coefficient gives ∫0∞​p2e−ap2dp=π​/(4a3/2). Therefore
n≃(h22πmkT​)3/2e(μ−mc2)/(kT)​.
(27)
The degeneracy factor here is the one in the supplied integral, namely one. Substituting kT=mc2/α, μ=0 and dividing by the supplied photon density gives
nγ​n​=8ζ(3)2π​​α3/2e−α​.
(28)
At α=20 this is about 4.8×10−8. The relic is already nonrelativistic at decoupling and becomes still colder as its momenta redshift, making it a possible cold dark matter component if it is stable and interacts sufficiently weakly with light.
For orientation, write ηb​=nb​/nγ​. Ignoring subsequent entropy transfer, its density relative to baryons would be ρX​/ρb​=(1/20)(n/nγ​)/ηb​. With the cosmological baryon-to-photon ratio of order 6×10−10, this is of order four, demonstrating the right cosmological scale. The measured dark-to-baryonic density ratio is likewise of order five; an observational reference is arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209 . This is a candidate abundance argument, not an exact relic-density calculation: photon heating after decoupling changes n/nγ​, and stability and interaction properties were not specified. The supplied mass and freeze-out parameter alone therefore do not establish a precise fit.

11H (Number Theory)

11H OurBigBook.com
For odd N>1 coprime to b, the Fermat pseudoprime test is bN−1≡1(modN). The Euler pseudoprime test meant here is the Euler–Jacobi test,
b(N−1)/2≡(Nb​)(modN),
(29)
where the right side is the Jacobi symbol. Write N−1=2sd, with d odd. The strong pseudoprime test passes when bd≡1, or when b2jd≡−1 for some 0≤j<s. Terminology often reserves “pseudoprime” for composite numbers; the question uses it for passing the respective test, including primes.
For the final example, 341=11⋅31 is composite and 210=1024≡1(mod341), so 2340≡1. It passes the Fermat primality test. However 2170≡1, whereas the supplementary law for the Jacobi symbol gives (2/341)=−1 since 341≡5(mod8). Thus 341 is Fermat but not Euler–Jacobi pseudoprime to base two. A weaker convention defining an Euler test merely by b(N−1)/2=±1 would not give the claimed distinction, which is why the Jacobi convention matters.

If N is prime, Fermat's little theorem gives b2sd≡1. If bd≡1, the strong test already passes. Otherwise let j≥1 be the first index with b2jd≡1. Its preceding value u=b2j−1d satisfies u2=1 and u=1 in the field FN​. Since (u−1)(u+1)=0 in a field, u=−1. The index j−1 lies between zero and s−1, so every coprime base passes the strong test when N is prime.

Words: 112
b OurBigBook.com
For the plain pseudoprime assertion use the Fermat primality test. In the finite group of units modulo an integer, let
L={b∈(Z/NZ)×:bN−1=1}.
(30)
It is the kernel of a group homomorphism, because the unit group is an abelian group. The given witness makes L a proper subgroup. By Lagrange's theorem for finite groups, ∣L∣≤φ(N)/2. Thus at least half of all units fail the test. Removing base one removes a passing base, so among the permitted 1<b<N there remain φ(N)−∣L∣ failures out of φ(N)−1 bases, still at least half.
The same argument works for the Euler–Jacobi test: its passing bases form the kernel of b↦b(N−1)/2(b/N)−1. One must not assert that strong-test passing bases form a subgroup; the kernel argument above concerns the Fermat statement requested here.

12F OurBigBook.com
The Lie group PSL(2,C) is a second-countable space. For every point of its discrete subgroup, choose the first basic neighbourhood isolating that point; different elements require different such neighbourhoods. This injects G into a countable set, proving countability.
A discrete subgroup is closed and meets compact sets in finitely many points. Indeed, distinct subgroup elements accumulating anywhere would give quotients converging to identity, contradicting an identity neighbourhood containing no other subgroup element. To apply this, use the positive Hermitian determinant-one model of hyperbolic space. At the base point I, the image under a determinant-one representative g is gg∗ and
2coshd(I,gg∗)=tr(gg∗)=∑i,j​∣gij​∣2.
(31)
This distance formula follows by unitary diagonalization: eigenvalues are et,e−t and the axial hyperbolic displacement is ∣t∣. Thus bounded displacement bounds all matrix entries. The determinant-one condition is closed, so the resulting set is compact; the quotient by {I,−I} is compact too. Conjugation gives the same conclusion at any base point. These are the bounded displacement sets of hyperbolic isometries are compact facts.
Hence, for each R, only finitely many g∈G satisfy d(p,gp)≤R. Any enumeration of an infinite group without repetitions therefore has d(p,gn​p)→∞. A finite discrete group is a harmless exception to the wording: it has no infinite enumeration of distinct elements, and proper discontinuity is immediate.
For a compact set C, put R=maxx∈C​d(p,x). If gC∩C=∅, choose x,gx∈C. The triangle inequality gives d(p,gp)≤d(p,gx)+d(x,p)≤2R. Only finitely many such g exist, proving properly discontinuous group action. Conversely, if the subgroup is not discrete, there are distinct gn​→e. A closed ball about p then meets its images under infinitely many gn​, violating this compact-set definition. Thus discreteness is equivalent to proper discontinuity. Here proper discontinuity allows finite point stabilizers; a stronger convention requiring freeness would exclude discrete elliptic subgroups and is not the equivalence intended.

The Gaussian log likelihood function, apart from a constant, is
ℓ(β,σ2)=−2n​logσ2−2σ2∥Y−Xβ∥2​.
(32)
Differentiating in β gives XT(Y−Xβ​)=0. Full column rank makes XTX invertible, so
β​=(XTX)−1XTY,β​∼Np​(β,σ2(XTX)−1)​.
(33)
The distribution follows by applying this linear map to the Gaussian error vector. Differentiating the profiled likelihood function in σ2 gives
σ2=n1​∥Y−Xβ​∥2​.
(34)
For its distribution, P=X(XTX)−1XT is symmetric idempotent, and the residual is (I−P)ϵ. The needed form of Cochran's theorem says that quadratic forms in a standard Gaussian vector associated with orthogonal symmetric projection matrices summing to identity are independent random variables with chi-squared distributions with degrees equal to their ranks. Applying it to P and I−P gives
σ2nσ2​∼χn−p2​​.
(35)
Thus the maximum-likelihood variance estimate uses divisor n and has expectation (n−p)σ2/n; the unbiased residual estimate would use divisor n−p. The fitted coefficient and residual quadratic form are also independent.

16H OurBigBook.com
A relation r on a set a is a well-founded relation when every nonempty subset b⊆a contains an element y with no x∈b satisfying xry. The well-founded recursion theorem states that a rule assigning a value at y from the already assigned values at its predecessors determines a unique function on a; the rule must give a unique set-valued output for every possible predecessor assignment. No choice or transitivity of r is needed.
Apply recursion with
f(y)=sup{f(x)+1:xry}.
(47)
The empty supremum is zero. Well-founded induction makes every value an ordinal; the Axiom schema of replacement collects the values into a set. Choose an ordinal α larger than every value. Then f:a→α, and xry implies f(x)+1≤f(y), hence f(x)<f(y).
Conversely, suppose such an ordinal-valued function exists. In any nonempty b⊆a, choose y∈b whose value is the least ordinal in f[b]. There can be no x∈b with xry, because it would have smaller value. Thus r is well-founded, proving the equivalence.
Using the axiom of choice, fix a well-order ≺ of a. Order its elements lexicographically by (f(x),x): first compare the ordinal rank, and for equal ranks use ≺. Every nonempty subset has a smallest rank and then a least element in that rank fibre, so this is a well-order. Since xry strictly increases rank, it respects every original relation pair. Hence every well-founded relation extends to a well-order under choice.

The denominator is positive in this nondegenerate convention. Otherwise all eigenvalues on the all-ones complement would coincide, forcing A=rI+(d−r)J/n. All off-diagonal entries would then be the same, making the graph complete or edgeless. For the triangle-free graph claim, suppose first there are at least two vertices. Nonadjacent vertices have a common neighbour, so the graph is connected. If u,v are adjacent, put U=N(u)∖{v} and V=N(v)∖{u}. Every member of U is nonadjacent to v, and exactly two of its three common neighbours with v lie in V, the third being u. By symmetry every member of V has exactly two neighbours in U. Counting these edges gives 2∣U∣=2∣V∣, hence d(u)=d(v). Connectivity makes the graph d-regular. Counting length-two paths from a vertex to non-neighbours gives
3(n−d−1)=d(d−1),n=1+d(d+2)/3​.
(51)
Here a=0, b=3, and the larger-root multiplicity becomes [n−1+d2/4d−3​]/2. Thus t=4d−3​ is rational and therefore an integer. It is odd, d=(t2+3)/4, and integrality also gives t∣d2. Since 16d2≡9(modt), one obtains t∣9, hence
t∈{1,3,9},d∈{1,3,21}​.

The complete bipartite graph K3,3​ realizes d=3: vertices in the same part have all three vertices of the other part as common neighbours, and vertices in opposite parts are adjacent. There are no triangles.
As literally worded, the one-vertex graph is a vacuous exception: it has no triangles or nonadjacent distinct pairs, but has d=0. The displayed positive-degree classification therefore requires at least two vertices. This qualification completes the triangle-free graphs with three common neighbours argument rather than silently excluding a counterexample.

Choose a nonzero vector in an irreducible representation. Its finite group orbit spans a finite-dimensional invariant subspace, which must be the whole representation. The representing matrices of an abelian group commute. Choose an eigenspace of one matrix; all other matrices preserve it. Repeatedly choosing an eigenspace for the restrictions of the remaining matrices gives a common eigenvector. Its line is invariant under the whole group. Irreducibility therefore makes the representation that line, proving every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is one-dimensional.

It is cyclic, and faithfulness makes A cyclic. Conversely a generator of a cyclic group of order m can be sent to e2πi/m, giving an injective one-dimensional character. Thus such a faithful representation exists exactly when A is a cyclic group.

A bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space is self-adjoint when T=T∗, equivalently ⟨Tx,y⟩=⟨x,Ty⟩. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators says its nonzero spectrum consists of real eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, with at most countably many and with accumulation possible only at zero. Their eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal; their closed span is the orthogonal complement of the kernel. On that span the operator has the norm-convergent spectral action Tx=∑j​λj​⟨x,ej​⟩ej​.
Take H=ℓ2(N) and Ten​=en​/n. It is self-adjoint and has infinite-dimensional range. Truncation to the first N coordinates is a finite-rank operator and differs from T in norm by 1/(N+1), so T is compact.
The resolvent set comprises those λ for which T−λI has a bounded everywhere-defined inverse; its complement is the spectrum, and the point spectrum consists of eigenvalues. In this example
σp​(T)={1/n:n≥1},σ(T)={0}∪{1/n:n≥1},ρ(T)=C∖σ(T)​.

For λ outside the displayed closed set the inverse is diagonal with entries (1/n−λ)−1 uniformly bounded, proving membership of the resolvent. Each 1/n has eigenvector en​. Zero is not an eigenvalue, but ∥Ten​∥→0 prevents a bounded inverse; also (1/n)n​∈ℓ2 has no preimage since that would be the non-square-summable constant sequence. MT​−MS​=∑k=0N−1​(Mk+1​−Mk​)1{S≤k<T}​.
(80)
For A∈FS​, the event A∩{S≤k<T} lies in Fk​. Every summand multiplied by its indicator therefore has expectation zero. Summing proves the conditional expectation identity. All terms are Lebesgue integrable since there are finitely many. Unbounded stopping requires an additional hypothesis such as uniform integrability of the stopped martingale; it is not justified solely by almost-sure finiteness.
The martingale convergence theorem ensures a finite almost-sure limit if supn​E∣Mn​∣<∞. Uniform integrability also gives convergence in L1. In particular bounded or nonnegative martingales satisfy the almost-sure convergence criterion. A symmetric random walk is a martingale but cannot have a finite limit, since each increment is ±1 and does not tend to zero. Some hypothesis is therefore necessary.
If there are j pessimists, the count increases with probability (K−j)j/[K(K−1)] and decreases with the identical probability. The remaining outcomes leave it unchanged, so Pn​=jn​/K is a bounded martingale. It converges almost surely. From any nonunanimous state, there is a fixed positive probability, bounded uniformly over the finitely many states, of reaching unanimity within K−1 steps by letting each other individual copy a chosen seed. Repeating blocks shows eventual absorption has probability one. Thus the finite voter-model consensus probability is
P∞​∈{0,1},P(P∞​=1)=P0​​.
(81)
The last equality follows from bounded convergence and the constant martingale expectation. The population eventually becomes wholly pessimistic or wholly optimistic, with probabilities equal to their respective initial proportions.

x(T)=W−∫0T​er(T−t)u(t)dt,W=erTx(0)+rA​(erT−1)>0.

u∗(t;μ)=μ−1e(β−r)(T−t)​.

μ∗=B/W​

For the constrained problem with no terminal reward, x(T)≥0 is exactly the weighted spending budget ∫er(T−t)u(t)dt≤W. The candidate u∗(⋅;μ∗) spends that budget exactly. This proves the requested optimality of the logarithmic spending with a terminal multiplier solution directly, including uniqueness up to changes on measure-zero sets.

A˙H​=ℏi​[HH​,AH​]​.

A spatial rotation is represented by UR​(θ)=exp[−iθn⋅J/ℏ], where J is the total angular momentum operator. For a particle J=L+S. The commutators [Ji​,xj​]=iℏϵijk​xk​ and [Ji​,Sj​]=iℏϵijk​Sk​ give
UR†​xUR​=x+θn×x+O(θ2),UR†​SUR​=S+θn×S+O(θ2).

Pa​=(coshκaκsinhκa​κ−1sinhκacoshκa​),D=(1−2λ​01​).
(97)
Their product has determinant one and trace 2[coshκa−(λ/κ)sinhκa]. Bloch theorem e±ika therefore give the negative-energy band of an attractive delta comb equation
coska=coshκa−κλ​sinhκa​.
(98)
Negative energies are allowed precisely where the right side lies in [−1,1]. A cell wavefunction can be written explicitly as
ψ(x)=ψ(0)sinhκasinhκ(a−x)+eikasinhκx​,0<x<a,

continued by Bloch theorem; the band equation enforces its derivative jump.
For λa≫1, the isolated well has κ=λ and energy E0​=−ℏ2λ2/(2m). Writing κ=λ+δ, the band equation gives δ∼2λe−λacoska. Hence
E(k)≃E0​−2tcoska,t=mℏ2λ2​e−λa​.

This is the nearest-neighbour tight-binding model. Its hopping magnitude follows independently from isolated wavefunctions ϕn​=λ​e−λ∣x−na∣: the neighbouring delta well contributes ⟨ϕ0​,(H−E0​)ϕ1​⟩≃−(ℏ2λ/m)ϕ0​(0)ϕ1​(0)=−t. The subtraction removes the overlap contribution of E0​. More distant contributions are exponentially smaller. For repulsive or absent wells, λ≤0, the quadratic form is nonnegative and there are no negative-energy bands.

Statistical temperature is defined by 1/T=(∂S/∂U)V,N​, with entropy S=kB​logΩ. Maximizing total entropy when two systems exchange energy makes their derivatives equal, explaining why equal temperature characterizes thermal equilibrium and why a thermometer can measure another system.
For a dilute monatomic ideal gas, Gaussian integration of momenta gives the classical partition function ZN​=VN/(N!λT3N​), with λT​=h/2πmkB​T​. Differentiating its logarithm gives
PV=NkB​T,U=23​NkB​T​.
(101)
At fixed volume, gas pressure is proportional to absolute temperature; at fixed pressure its volume is proportional to temperature. A low-density gas thermometer therefore supplies an absolute calibration independent of the gas species in the ideal limit. A liquid-in-glass column responds to the difference between liquid and glass thermal expansion, which need not be exactly linear. Calibration against gas temperatures and correction for expansion nonlinearities improve a simple two-point column scale; an ideal-gas law is not a law of the liquid itself.
For blackbody radiation, the electromagnetic mode density is 8πν2/c3 per volume and frequency interval, including two polarizations. For one photon mode, summing its occupation numbers gives Zν​=∑j≥0​e−jhν/(kB​T)=(1−e−hν/(kB​T))−1. Differentiation of logZν​ gives mean energy hν/(ehν/kB​T−1), so the Planck distribution follows. Converting to wavelength gives spectral radiance
Bλ​(T)=λ52hc2​ehc/(λkB​T)−11​.
(102)
At its maximum, z=hc/(λkB​T) satisfies 5(1−e−z)=z, whose positive root is 4.9651…. Thus the Wien displacement law is
λmax​T=4.9651…kB​hc​≃2.898×10−3 mK​.
(103)
This calibrates a wavelength-based radiation thermometer and avoids identifying a subjective colour with a universal temperature. A peak per frequency interval has a different numerical location, so the spectral convention must be stated. Real objects require emissivity and atmospheric corrections; fitting a measured spectrum is more informative than choosing its visually brightest colour. Integrating the Planck distribution also gives energy density proportional to T4 and radiative flux proportional to T4, supplying the complementary Stefan–Boltzmann law calibration.

ϕ(t,x)=4πϵ0​q​R∗​−v∗​⋅R∗​1​​,R∗​=x−x0​(t∗​),R∗​=∣R∗​∣.

Normal coordinates at an event have gab​=ηab​ and first metric derivatives, equivalently connection coefficients, zero there. They describe freely falling frames in which nongravitational laws take their special-relativistic form to first order, expressing the Equivalence principle. Curvature and tidal effects cannot generally be removed throughout a neighbourhood.
For a covector, ∇a​Vb​=∂a​Vb​−Γabc​Vc​. The Levi-Civita connection is torsion-free, so
∂a​Vb​−∂b​Va​=∇a​Vb​−∇b​Va​
(107)
is an antisymmetric covariant tensor. Next expand ∇a​Kb​+∇b​Ka​ using Kb​=gbc​Kc and 2gcd​Γabd​=∂a​gbc​+∂b​gac​−∂c​gab​. Cancelling the first two metric derivatives leaves
2∇(a​Kb)​=Kc∂c​gab​+gac​∂b​Kc+gbc​∂a​Kc=Qab​​.
(108)
If K=∂4​ has constant coordinate components, Qab​=∂4​gab​. Thus Q=0 implies the metric is independent of x4 and K is a Killing vector. Its derivative is antisymmetric, yielding
∇a​Kb​=21​(∂a​Kb​−∂b​Ka​)​.
(109)
For an affinely parametrized geodesic with tangent u, differentiation gives
dλd​(−Ka​ua)=−uaub∇a​Kb​−Ka​∇u​ua=0.
(110)
The first term vanishes by antisymmetry and the second by the geodesic equation, proving conservation in every coordinate system. A stationary metric requires the Killing vector to be timelike in the region concerned. For particle energy, the tangent should be future timelike for a massive particle, with affine parameter proportional to proper time, or future null with appropriate momentum normalization for a photon; normalize the future timelike Killing vector relative to the chosen stationary observers or at infinity. Then the conserved quantity is proportional to their Killing energy. A spacelike Killing vector instead represents momentum, not stationary time translation.

For a physical adiabatic ideal gas one has γ>1; the following algebra also holds for positive γ=1. Compression work implies p=ρW′(ρ)−W, obtained by differentiating the total internal energy VW(M/V) at fixed mass. With the stated pressure law this integrates to
W(ρ)=p/(γ−1)+Cρ​.

The term proportional to mass is an arbitrary energy reference; set C=0. Mass flux is ρu, momentum flux is p+ρu2, and dividing the energy flux by mass flux gives
γ−1γ​ρp​+2u2​=constant​

for steady flow.
Work in the shock's rest frame. If the shock speed in the laboratory is D, upstream speed relative to it is D and downstream speed is D/r, where r=ρ1​/ρ0​. Conservation of momentum gives p1​−p0​=ρ0​D2(1−1/r). Conservation of specific total enthalpy gives
γ−1γ​ρ0​p0​​+2D2​=γ−1γ​rρ0​p1​​+2r2D2​.
(117)
Eliminating D2 and using p1​/p0​=1+β yields
ρ0​ρ1​​=2γ+(γ−1)β2γ+(γ+1)β​​.
(118)
Its weak-shock expansion is 1+β/γ−(γ−1)β2/(2γ2)+O(β3), exactly the expansion of (1+β)1/γ through second order. Thus the adiabatic pressure-density relation agrees to order β2; entropy production first affects this comparison at higher order. The same isentropic constant is not exactly preserved across a finite shock. The wording allows γ=1, but the printed enthalpy formula is then undefined. The compression calculation instead gives W=(p0​/ρ0​)ρlog(ρ/ρ0​)+Cρ, and the specific enthalpy is (p0​/ρ0​)[1+log(ρ/ρ0​)]+C. Thus the requested formula containing 1/(γ−1) requires γ=1; its physical ideal-gas application uses γ>1.
